hints: Focus on the cell type: bone marrow stem cells must divide by mitosis very many times in a lifetime, so think about what happens to the ends of chromosomes with every division.
Recall the normal job of telomerase in stem cells: rebuilding telomeres to prevent chromosome shortening, then ask what must happen if that rebuilding cannot occur.
walkthrough:
**Recall what telomerase does**

Think of telomeres as protective caps on the ends of chromosomes. A little bit is lost every time DNA is copied in mitosis.

Normal rule in stem cells:
$$telomerase \ rebuilds \ telomeres \ so \ division \ can \ continue$$

**Apply the mutation**

Here the mutation prevents any telomerase being made. So with each stem cell division, the telomeres just get shorter and shorter with no repair.

**Link to stem cell fate**

Bone marrow stem cells need to keep dividing to make all blood cells. Once telomeres become critically short, the cell stops the cycle to protect its DNA. So eventually the stem cells can no longer divide, which is option C.

options.A: Loss of telomerase does not stimulate division, it limits it, so lymphocyte production would fall not rapidly increase.
options.B: A tumour needs uncontrolled division, but without telomerase division is stopped sooner, so this is the opposite effect.
options.C: Without telomerase, telomeres shorten each mitosis until a critical length triggers cell cycle arrest, so stem cells eventually stop dividing.
options.D: If stem cells stop dividing they cannot replace red cells, white cells and platelets, so total blood cell count must fall.
